system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 3 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 40-60 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2185-11-23 09:59:00 to 2185-11-25 11:30:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A male patient with a history of mitochondrial myopathy, autonomic dysfunction, and coronary artery disease was admitted for chest pressure, hypertension, and generalized weakness. His symptoms began over the weekend with elevated blood pressure and headache, which partially improved with rest. He presented to his primary care provider with new-onset chest pressure, nausea, and reduced oral intake. Evaluation revealed no acute cardiac ischemia, with normal EKG and undetectable troponin. A chest X-ray showed no acute cardiopulmonary process. He was treated with IV fluids, leading to resolution of chest pressure and improvement in orthostatic symptoms. His outpatient cardiologist, neurologist, and mitochondrial specialist were consulted; no new therapies were recommended due to his initial hypertension. Outpatient IV hydration was arranged closer to his home. He was discharged asymptomatic with continued management focused on hydration and monitoring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning, Mr. Thompson. I'm Dr. Lee, one of the hospitalists. You're here today for your IVIG infusion because of your low immune globulin levels, correct?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s right. I’ve been getting these infusions every few months. I usually do okay, but sometimes I react to new treatments, so they like to monitor me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. We’ll keep a close eye on you. How are you feeling today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Pretty much my usual self. I’ve been a bit dehydrated lately—had some loose, explosive stools yesterday and this morning. But that’s not unusual for me. My bowels go back and forth between diarrhea and constipation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thanks for letting me know. No fever, nausea, or vomiting?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, nothing like that. Just felt a little off yesterday morning, but it passed quickly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And any chest pain or shortness of breath?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Not really—well, maybe a little shortness of breath about an hour ago. But I think it’s just from being a bit dehydrated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Got it. We’ll check your labs and start you on IV fluids to help with that. We’ll also give your IVIG infusion around noon. Any allergies we should watch for?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes—sulfa, tetracycline, iodine, shellfish, ACE inhibitors, ciprofloxacin, NSAIDs, prednisone, IV dye, and cortisone. I’ve had reactions before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Noted. We’ll avoid those. Let me go over your meds too. You’re on atorvastatin, Plavix, Nexium, Zetia, metoprolol, ranolazine, valsartan, and aspirin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s all correct. And ferrous gluconate for iron.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll continue all of those. We’ve already drawn blood—your kidney function is a little elevated, creatinine at 1.4, but stable for you. We’ll keep an eye on it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, that’s normal for me. My mitochondrial disease affects my kidneys when I get dehydrated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Understood. We’re giving you normal saline to help with that. Your IVIG will start in about 45 minutes. I’ll check back after it begins.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How are you feeling now that the IVIG has been running for about 15 minutes?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay so far. My blood pressure feels a little high—I’ve got a mild headache.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We noticed that—your BP is 148/90. It’s a bit up from your baseline, but not alarming. We’ll monitor it. Any chest pain, rash, or difficulty breathing?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, nothing like that. Just the headache.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep going slowly. Let me know if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How did you sleep? Any issues overnight?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I woke up with some chest pressure and shortness of breath. My blood pressure was really high—felt awful for a bit.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Did you use your nitroglycerin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I took one under my tongue. The chest pressure eased up after a few minutes, and my BP came down too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. We checked an EKG—it’s unchanged from your baseline, no signs of a heart attack. We’ve done three sets of cardiac enzymes, all negative. So no heart damage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. But then I felt nauseous later. They gave me Zofran and Compazine, and that helped.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we saw that. No vomiting, though?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, just nausea. I’m feeling much better now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your telemetry showed no arrhythmias, and your repeat labs are stable. The chest pressure and nausea may have been a reaction related to your mitochondrial condition or blood pressure fluctuation. We’re continuing your IV fluids—4 liters total during your stay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. I’ve had episodes like this before when I’m dehydrated or stressed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep monitoring you today. If you continue to improve, we may be able to discharge you tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re looking well. How are you feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel back to my usual self. No chest pressure, no nausea, breathing fine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. Your labs are stable, and your heart enzymes stayed negative. The EKG didn’t change. We believe the episode was likely due to hypertension and dehydration, not a heart attack.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the IVIG—I tolerated it okay, aside from the next day’s symptoms?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you got the full 30 grams. The reaction the next day isn’t uncommon, especially with your history. We’ll note that for future infusions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. So can I go home today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re clearing you for discharge. No changes to your meds. Continue everything as before. Stay hydrated, especially with your mitochondrial condition.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do. Thanks for keeping an eye on me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. If you have chest pain that doesn’t respond to nitroglycerin, or severe shortness of breath, go to the ER. Otherwise, follow up with your specialists as planned.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. I’ll stay in touch with my mitochondrial and heart doctors.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. We’ll get your discharge papers ready. You should be out within the hour.

summary.summary_paragraph: A male patient with a history of mitochondrial myopathy, coronary artery disease, and hypogammaglobulinemia was admitted for monitored IVIG infusion due to prior intolerance of new treatments. He reported mild dehydration and recent diarrhea but was otherwise in his usual state of health. On hospital day one, he received 30 grams of IVIG with only mild hypertension. On day two, he developed transient chest pressure and shortness of breath associated with elevated blood pressure, which resolved with sublingual nitroglycerin and antihypertensive effect. Serial cardiac enzymes were negative and EKG unchanged, ruling out acute myocardial infarction. He also experienced nausea, resolved with antiemetics. He received 4 liters of IV normal saline for hydration support. By hospital day three, he was asymptomatic and requested discharge. No medication changes were made. He was discharged home in stable condition with instructions to continue baseline therapies and maintain hydration.
